title: HTML Images
summary: An image element displays a picture, and alt text explains its purpose.

subtopics.title: The document frame
subtopics.explanation: `src` gives the browser the image location, such as `/images/forest.jpg`. It is like writing the storage address on a delivery request. Use a path that works after deployment, and choose an appropriately sized image so visitors do not download a huge file for a small thumbnail. For example, for a meaningful product photo, describe the product detail the surrounding text does not already say. For example, describe the useful content of a product photo rather than its filename.

subtopics.title: Important pieces
subtopics.explanation: `alt` describes the useful information an image contributes in its context. It should be concise and should not start with “image of” unless that matters. It is like a short caption read aloud. If the image is a link, describe the link’s purpose where appropriate. For example, if the image is the only content in a link, its alternative text should name the destination or action. For example, use empty alt text for a purely decorative image.

subtopics.title: Page information
subtopics.explanation: A decorative image adds no information needed to understand the page. Use `alt=""` so assistive technology can skip it. This is like leaving a background flourish out of a spoken description. Do not omit the attribute, because the browser may expose the file name instead. For example, an empty alt value is appropriate for a decorative divider that carries no message. For example, reserve image dimensions so a list does not jump as thumbnails load.

subtopics.title: Content structure
subtopics.explanation: `width` and `height` let the browser reserve the image’s shape before the file loads. This reduces content jumping as the image appears. It is like leaving a space for a poster before hanging it. Preserve the image’s proportions or pair it with `object-fit` when the design crops it. For example, for a wide image shown in a narrow card, reserve its ratio and use object-fit only when cropping is acceptable. For example, use object-fit for a fixed card only after checking what the crop removes.

subtopics.title: Good habits
subtopics.explanation: Wrap an image in a link only when activating the image should navigate somewhere. In that case, the link needs an accessible name that explains its destination. It is like making a poster into a doorway: people need to know where it leads. Keep decorative images out of the focus order. For example, use a smaller responsive source for a phone when downloading the original would waste data. For example, if an image is the only content of a link, name its destination accessibly.

foundations.overview: The `` element displays an image file in a page. `src` locates the file; `alt` supplies a text equivalent when the image carries information. Think of an image as a poster with a written caption for someone who cannot see it. Reserve its dimensions to reduce layout shifts, use suitable file sizes, and make decorative images skippable.
foundations.whyItMatters: Images affect page weight, layout stability, and accessibility. Source selection and alternative text should match the image’s role in the surrounding content.
commonUseCases: A news article needs alternative text for its informative lead image.
A logo that links home needs an accessible link name.
A decorative background image should not create extra spoken content.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Adding alt text is optional when the image has a filename.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A filename rarely explains the image’s purpose; meaningful images need useful alternative text.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every image needs a detailed description.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Decorative images should be skipped, while informative images need concise context.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Width and height only affect visual styling.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They also reserve layout space and can prevent content from jumping while an image loads.

visualExplorer.title: How the browser loads an
visualExplorer.caption: From parsing the tag to picking a candidate and reserving space, here's the lifecycle of an image load.

config.intro: An tag triggers a multi-step process: the browser must decide which file to fetch, reserve layout space, fetch it (now or later), then paint it.

steps.name: Parse the tag
steps.detail: The parser encounters and reads its attributes: src, alt, width, height, srcset, sizes, loading.

steps.name: Reserve space
steps.detail: If width/height (or CSS aspect-ratio) are present, the browser reserves the correct box immediately so nothing shifts later (good CLS).

steps.name: Pick a candidate
steps.detail: If srcset/sizes are set, the browser evaluates viewport width and pixel density to choose the best-sized file.

steps.name: Fetch (now or lazy)
steps.detail: Without loading='lazy', the request starts right away. With it, the fetch is deferred until the image nears the viewport.

steps.name: Decode & paint
steps.detail: The browser decodes the image and paints it into the reserved box. If it fails, the alt text is shown instead.

interactiveExamples.title: A basic image with alt text
interactiveExamples.explanation: The minimum responsible image: src, descriptive alt, and width/height to reserve space. Notice the alt describes what the image shows, not that it 'is an image'.

files.index.html:
Our Mascot

Setting width and height reserves space so the text below doesn't jump.
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 20px; }
img { border-radius: 8px; max-width: 100%; height: auto; }

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A heading, a kitten image with rounded corners, and a paragraph below it that does not jump as the image loads.

interactiveExamples.title: Decorative vs content images
interactiveExamples.explanation: The first image conveys information and gets descriptive alt. The second is a decorative divider, so it uses alt="" and screen readers skip it.

files.index.html:
Trip report

The thin grey bar above is decorative — its alt is empty.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A photo with meaningful alt text, then a thin decorative divider that assistive tech ignores.

interactiveExamples.title: Modern formats with <picture>
interactiveExamples.explanation: The browser tries each in order and uses the first type it supports, falling back to the if none match. This serves AVIF/WebP to modern browsers and JPEG to old ones.

files.index.html: Modern browsers grab AVIF/WebP; older ones fall back to the JPEG.
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 20px; }
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; border-radius: 8px; }

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A single rendered image — the browser silently chose the best supported format from the <picture> sources.

codeLab.title: Make an image accessible and stable
codeLab.instructions: This is missing alt text and width/height. Add a descriptive alt attribute and the intrinsic width (600) and height (400) so the layout doesn't shift.

files.index.html:
Beach Day

Some text below the image.
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 16px; }
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }

codeLab.expectedOutput: The same image, but now with descriptive alt text and reserved space (no layout jump).

files.index.html:
Beach Day

Some text below the image.
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 16px; }
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }

hints: alt should describe what the image shows, not start with 'image of'.
Add width="600" and height="400" so the browser reserves the right box before the image downloads.

codeLab.title: Add responsive sources with srcset
codeLab.instructions: Add a srcset so phones download a 480px-wide file and large screens download a 1200px-wide file, plus a sizes hint that the image displays full-width up to 600px, then at 1200px.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A responsive image where the browser chooses the best-sized file for the screen.
hints: srcset lists files with their intrinsic widths using the 'w' descriptor (e.g. 480w).
sizes tells the browser how wide the image renders at each breakpoint so it can pick a candidate before layout.

keyTakeaways: `src` gives the browser the image location, such as `/images/forest.
`alt` describes the useful information an image contributes in its context.
A decorative image adds no information needed to understand the page.
`width` and `height` let the browser reserve the image’s shape before the file loads.
Wrap an image in a link only when activating the image should navigate somewhere.
